clue.text: After hostile takeover, almost everyone's concerned with employment

indicators.note: the piece for almost everyone is placed after the takeover piece

parts.note: an occupation is the seizure of a territory or building by force, a hostile takeover

indicators.note: almost means the final letter of the word for everyone is dropped

parts.note: everyone means all; the 's is a link meaning 'is'

explanation.surface: A business commentator notes that after a hostile bid, nearly everyone is worried about their job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hostile takeover' reads as corporate jargon, but it means a military occupation; 'After' only fixes the order of the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Occupational describes things relating to a person's job or trade, so it means to do with employment.

clue.text: Running bar offering a large range of items

definitions.text: offering a large range of items

parts.note: a machine that is running is on
to estop is a legal term meaning to bar or preclude

explanation.surface: A bar that keeps going serves a wide variety of drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: ESTOP, a legal verb meaning to bar (as in estoppel), is the obscure part.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-stop shop or service provides everything a customer needs in a single place.

clue.text: Bismarck briefly detained in prison building

indicators.note: detained in places the shortened name inside the word for prison

parts.note: a cage is a place of confinement

indicators.note: briefly means the name loses its final letter

parts.note: Otto von Bismarck was the German chancellor

explanation.surface: The German chancellor, held for a short time, is locked up in a jail block.
explanation.walkthrough: Bismarck's first name was Otto; 'briefly' is the usual signal to drop a final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A cottage is a small house, a kind of building.

clue.text: Death caps put paid to dancer's move

indicators.note: putting paid to something destroys it, so the letters are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: Poisonous mushrooms ended a ballet dancer's career.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Death caps' are toadstools, but here they are just the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A pas de chat is a ballet leap, literally a cat's step, so it is a dancer's movement.

clue.text: Project worth developing

indicators.note: developing means changing form, so the letters of worth are rearranged

explanation.surface: A scheme seems worth working up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Project' looks like a noun, but it is the verb to throw.
explanation.definitionFit: To project something is to throw or hurl it forward.

clue.text: Top solicitor with job in remote settlement

indicators.note: to top something is to cut off its head, so the first letter goes

parts.note: a tout solicits custom, as a ticket tout does
a post is a position or job

explanation.surface: A leading lawyer takes a position somewhere far away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top solicitor' looks like a leading lawyer, but 'Top' is a verb: behead TOUT to leave OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: An outpost is a small settlement or station in a remote or frontier area.

clue.text: Firm employs a worker to fix blockage

indicators.note: to fix here means to hold in place, so the a and worker pieces enclose the blockage

parts.note: a worker is a worker ant, so ant
a dam is a barrier blocking a river

explanation.surface: A company hires someone to clear an obstruction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like a company, but it is the adjective; 'to fix' means to hold firmly in place, so the worker and the a hold the blockage.
explanation.definitionFit: Adamant means unshakeable in purpose, firm in one's position.

clue.text: Works with MI6 to protect English members of the ruling class

parts.note: a works or factory is a plant

indicators.note: to protect means the spies' word wraps around the abbreviation for English

parts.note: MI6 is the British secret intelligence service, staffed by agents

explanation.surface: Factories collaborate with British intelligence to guard English aristocrats.
explanation.walkthrough: The Plantagenets were the royal house that ruled England from 1154 to 1485; 'Works' looks like a verb but is a factory.
explanation.definitionFit: The Plantagenets were a dynasty of English kings, literally members of a ruling house.

clue.text: Man at Danish court determined to take most of country back

indicators.note: back says the combined pieces are read in reverse order, last letter first

parts.note: a determined or fixed thing is set

indicators.note: most of drops the final letter of the word for country

parts.note: a realm is a kingdom or country

explanation.surface: A man at the Danish court is resolved to seize most of a land back again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns round the whole run of both pieces. The Danish court is Elsinore in Hamlet, where Laertes is Polonius's son.
explanation.definitionFit: Laertes is a courtier at Elsinore in Shakespeare's Hamlet, the Danish court of the play.

clue.text: Gunners getting draw in competition

parts.note: RA is the Royal Artillery, the army's gunners
to draw a line or outline is to trace it

explanation.surface: Artillerymen secure a tied result in a contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'draw' looks like a tied match, but it is the verb to trace.
explanation.definitionFit: The rat race is the fierce struggle for success and advancement in working life, a form of competition.

clue.text: Get into exercises right away for fun

parts.note: to get into a room is to enter it

indicators.note: away signals the letter for right is removed

parts.note: training is a course of exercises

explanation.surface: Someone takes up workouts straight away for enjoyment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right away' looks like 'immediately', but it removes R from TRAINING, giving TAINING.
explanation.definitionFit: Something entertaining is amusing, so the adjective fun is a fair synonym.

clue.text: Teachers cover for fool

parts.note: NUT is the National Union of Teachers, a British teaching union
a case is a protective cover or container

explanation.surface: Staff standing in for one another are dismissed as idiots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cover' suggests a supply teacher standing in, but it is CASE. The NUT was the main British teachers' union.
explanation.definitionFit: A nutcase is an informal word for a crazy or foolish person.

clue.text: Court poet mostly a social creature

parts.note: to court someone is to woo them

indicators.note: mostly signals the poet's name loses its final letter

parts.note: Dante is the Italian poet of the Divine Comedy

explanation.surface: A royal court's versifier is largely a gregarious sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' reads as a royal court, but it is the verb woo.
explanation.definitionFit: The wood ant is a colonial insect, and ants are classic social insects living in organised nests.

clue.text: Fruit with spots on skin needs to be peeled

indicators.note: peeling removes the outer layer, so the word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: dappled means marked with spots or patches, as on a horse's coat

explanation.surface: A piece of fruit with blemished skin ought to be peeled before eating.
explanation.walkthrough: DAPPLED loses its outer Ds when 'peeled'.
explanation.definitionFit: An apple is a common orchard fruit.

clue.text: Relax during warm weather or … I just can't decide

indicators.note: during places the word for relax inside the word for warm weather

parts.note: heat is hot or warm weather
to sit, as in sit back, is to relax
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone dithers between lounging in the sunshine or doing something else.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins the wordplay to the definition, which is a speaker's own words rather than a description.
explanation.definitionFit: A hesitator is someone who hesitates, exactly the person who would say they cannot make up their mind.

clue.text: Group of pupils allowed running water

parts.note: in British schools a stream is a group of pupils of similar ability
let means allowed

explanation.surface: A class of schoolchildren are permitted to play in the brook.
explanation.walkthrough: In British schools, pupils are 'streamed' into ability groups called streams.
explanation.definitionFit: A streamlet is a small stream, a trickle of running water.

clue.text: Minor player's debut in concert seen by rock fan

parts.note: an extra is a minor player in a film crowd scene; the 's is a link

indicators.note: the debut of a word is its first letter

parts.note: a tor is a rocky peak, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A bit-part actor's first appearance at a concert is watched by an enthusiastic follower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fan' looks like an admirer, but it is the machine. A TOR is a rocky hill in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: An extractor fan is a fan that draws stale air or fumes out of a room, often called simply an extractor.

clue.text: Evict number of people present

definitions.meaning: to throw someone out of their home
the attendance at an event or election

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is the phrasal verb 'turn out'; the second the noun, as in a high turnout at the polls.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn out is to expel someone, and a turnout is the count of those attending.

clue.text: Germany in trouble over supporting a North African republic

indicators.note: in a down entry the lower piece supports the one above, so the a comes first
in places the abbreviation for Germany inside the turned word
over in a down clue means the word is turned upside down

parts.note: to ail is to trouble or afflict

explanation.surface: Germany is in difficulty over backing an African state.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' turns AIL upside down, giving LIA; 'supporting' puts the a on top of the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Algeria is a republic on the North African coast.

clue.text: Bones: principal ingredients of stock as cook regularly avers

indicators.note: the principal or leading part of each word is its initial letter

explanation.surface: A recipe note claims the main elements of a stock are bones, as any regular cook would affirm.
explanation.walkthrough: The initials of all five words from 'stock' to 'avers' spell the answer; 'regularly' is not an alternate-letter signal here.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacra is the plural of sacrum, the triangular bone at the base of the spine.

clue.text: Enclosing extra money, dispatch payment

indicators.note: enclosing means one word is wrapped around another, as in an envelope

parts.note: to dispatch is to send
a tip is extra money given for service

explanation.surface: Someone posts a payment with a bonus tucked inside.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures money tucked into a posted envelope, which is exactly how the container works.
explanation.definitionFit: A stipend is a fixed regular payment, such as a salary or allowance.

clue.text: Prisoner accepted pardon

parts.note: con is slang for a convict, a prisoner
done means accepted, as in 'it's not done'

explanation.surface: A convict receives a pardon.
explanation.definitionFit: To condone is to overlook or forgive an offence, much as one might pardon it.

clue.text: Infuriates sergeant terribly, failing to keep time

indicators.note: terribly suggests the letters of sergeant are mangled into a new order
failing to keep a letter means it is dropped from the mix

explanation.surface: A sergeant is driven mad by his own lateness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terribly' scrambles SERGEANT, and 'failing to keep' removes its T.
explanation.definitionFit: To enrage someone is to make them furious, which is what infuriates means.

clue.text: Children's programmes entertain me

indicators.note: to entertain is to hold or harbour, so the run is held within the words

explanation.surface: A child says kids' television keeps them amused.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue speaks as the answer: 'me' is the child, a sprog, held in 'Children's programmes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprog is British slang for a child, so 'me' is the child speaking for itself.

clue.text: A French wine, good little number stocked in this town?

indicators.note: stocked in places the good and number pieces inside the wine word

parts.note: vin is the French word for wine
No is the short form of number

explanation.surface: A French wine and a decent small item are kept in a certain town.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as loose: Avignon is a southern French city in wine country, home to the Côtes du Rhône.
explanation.definitionFit: Avignon is a historic city in Provence, a fitting place to stock French wine.

clue.text: I'll search high and low for a cleaner

definitions.meaning: one who scours, searching a place thoroughly, would say this
a pad or brush used for scrubbing pots clean

explanation.walkthrough: Both senses come from the verb scour: to search thoroughly and to scrub hard.
explanation.definitionFit: A scourer is both a person who scours an area and an abrasive pad for scrubbing pans.

clue.text: Taken outside I have to rest

indicators.note: outside puts the word for taken around the letter I

parts.note: led means taken somewhere, as one leads a child to school
to own something is to have it

explanation.surface: Someone escorted out of the room needs a lie-down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken outside' sounds like being escorted out, but it is the container signal around the I.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie down is to recline and rest.

clue.text: Get this grade after much revision as a rule

indicators.note: heavy revision reworks the letters of the phrase into a new order

explanation.surface: A student earns a certain mark only after lots of study as a matter of course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revision' sounds like exam study but signals the rearrangement; 'rule' looks like a regulation but is a ruler.
explanation.definitionFit: A straightedge is a ruler or bar used for drawing or checking straight lines.
